source_text: Quanta vero de diis vestris animalia muta naturaliter judicant? Mures, hirundines, milvi, non sentire eos sciunt, norunt; inculcant, insident; ac, nisi abigatis, in ipso dei vestri ore nidificant. Araneae vero faciem ejus intexunt, et de ipso capite sua fila suspendunt: vos tergitis, mundatis, eraditis, et illos quos facitis, protegitis et timetis. Dum unusquisque vestrum non cogitat prius se debere Deum nosse quam colere; dum inconsulte gestiunt parentibus obedire; dum fieri malunt alieni erroris accessio, quam sibi credere; dum nihil ex his quae timent norunt: sic in auro et argento avaritia consecrata est; sic statuarum inanium consignata forma; sic nata Romana superstitio. Quorum ritus si percenseas, ridenda quam multa, [multa] etiam miseranda sunt. Nudi cruda hieme discurrunt; alii incedunt pileati, scuta vetera circumferunt, pelles caedunt mendicantes, vicantes deos ducunt. Quaedam fana semel anno adire permittunt, quaedam in totum nefas visere; est quo viro non licet, nonnulla absque feminis sacra sunt; etiam servo quibusdam caerimonis interesse piaculare flagitium est: alia sacra coronat univira, alia multivira, et magna religione conquiritur quae plura possit adulteria numerare. Quid? qui sanguine suo libat et vulneribus suis supplicat, non profanus melius esset, quam sic religiosus? aut cui exta sunt obscoena demessa, quomodo Deum violat, qui hoc modo placat, quum, si eunuchos Deus vellet, posset procreare, non facere? Quis non intelligat male sanos, et vanae et perditae mentis in ista desipere, et ipsam errantium turbam mutua sibi patrocinia praestare? heic defensio communis furoris est furentium multitudo.
pass_a_gloss: How much indeed mute animals naturally judge about your gods? Mice, swallows, kites, they do not perceive them, they know; they tread on them, they perch on them; and, unless you drive them away, they nest in the very mouth of your god. Spiders indeed weave their web on his face, and from his very head they suspend their threads: you sweep, you clean, you eradicate, and those things which you make, you protect and fear. While each one of you does not think beforehand that he ought to know God before worshiping; while they strive to obey parents without consideration; while they prefer to become an addition to someone else's error rather than believe for themselves; while they know nothing from those things which they fear: thus avarice is consecrated in gold and silver; thus the form of empty statues is dedicated; thus Roman superstition was born. If you should examine the rites of these, how many are laughable, and also pitiable. Some run about naked in raw winter; others proceed wearing felt hats, carrying old shields, striking hides, begging, leading gods in procession. Certain temples they permit to be approached only once a year; certain ones it is entirely wrong to visit; there is something which is not permitted to a man, some sacred rites are without women; and it is also a sacrilegious fault for a slave to participate in certain ceremonies: one sacred rite is crowned by a single wife, another by many wives, and with great religiosity that which can count more adulteries is sought. What? He who offers libation with his own blood and supplicates with his own wounds, would he not be better as a non-believer than thus religious? Or to whom the entrails are an abomination cast away, how does he violate God, who thus placates, since, if God wanted eunuchs, he could produce, not make? Who does not understand that the poorly sane, and the vain and lost mind, are foolish in these things, and the very crowd of the erring provides mutual defenses for themselves? This defense is the common frenzy of the multitude of the frenzied.

pass_b_english: Consider how mute animals instinctively pass judgment on your gods. Mice, swallows, and kites neither perceive nor acknowledge them; they tread upon them, perch on them, and unless you drive them off, they even build nests right inside your god's mouth. Spiders weave their webs across his face and hang their threads from his very head. Yet you sweep, clean, and eradicate those webs, even while you protect and fear the statues you yourselves have made.

So long as each of you fails to grasp that you must know God before you can worship him; so long as you strive to obey your parents without thought; so long as you prefer to join someone else's error rather than believe for yourselves; so long as you understand nothing of the very things you fear—thus avarice is consecrated in gold and silver, thus the form of empty statues is dedicated, and thus Roman superstition was born.

If you examine the rites of these gods, you will find much that is laughable and much that is pitiable. Some participants run naked through the raw winter; others march in felt caps, lugging old shields, slashing hides, begging, and parading their gods in procession. Certain temples may be entered only once a year; others are utterly forbidden to visit. Some rites bar men entirely; others exclude women. For a slave to take part in certain ceremonies is a sacrilegious crime. One rite is presided over by a woman married once, another by a woman married many times, and with great religious fervor they seek out the one who can count the most adulteries.

What of the man who pours out his own blood as a libation and begs with his own wounds? Would he not be better off as an unbeliever than religious in such a way? Or the man who casts away the entrails as an abomination—how does he violate God by placating him in this manner, since if God had wanted eunuchs, he could have created them rather than requiring men to make them? Who fails to see that unsound minds, vain and lost, act foolishly in these things, and that the very crowd of the erring provides mutual cover for one another? This defense is nothing but the common frenzy of a frenzied multitude.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex conditional clauses and the rhetorical questions. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The distinction in the eunuch clause ('posset procreare, non facere') is correctly handled in both versions.
